opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The way I see it, digital work is going to move first and move much faster, simply because bits are so much easier to manipulate than atoms. When everything lives in a computer, you can iterate incredibly quickly. You can copy and paste, run things in parallel, undo mistakes, and the cost of experimentation is basically compute. So a huge amount of knowledge work is going to get automated or heavily augmented well before we see the same thing in the physical world.

The physical world is just much harder. You have to build hardware, deal with supply chains, manufacturing, and safety, and the environment is really messy and long-tailed. Having worked on self-driving at Tesla, I've seen firsthand how long it takes to get from a demo that works 90% of the time to something you can actually deploy, where every additional nine of reliability is a ton of work. Driving is just one narrow task, and it took over a decade. Robotics more generally is going to have a similar flavor, maybe compressed somewhat because the underlying models are much better now.

So I'd describe it as a progression. First there's a massive wave of digital transformation, where agents and LLMs do a lot of the information processing. Then there's an interface layer between the digital and the physical, things like sensors, cameras, and actuators, where the digital intelligence starts to read from and write to the world. Eventually the physical world itself opens up, and that's probably the biggest market by far, because so much of the economy is ultimately atoms. But it lags, and it'll be capital intensive and slower than people expect.

One thing I'd add is that I think humanoids and general-purpose robots are a very reasonable bet. The world is built for humans, so a human form factor lets you plug into all the existing infrastructure. I'm excited about it, but I'd encourage people to keep realistic timelines. The digital opportunities are here now, and the physical ones are coming, just with a lot more friction along the way.

r002.rationale: It says the physical world is “probably the biggest market by far,” explicitly comparing its potential with the earlier digital transformation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I've come to see it is that there's a pretty clear ordering here, and it's basically dictated by where the data is and how cheap it is to iterate.

Digital work goes first because it's just overwhelmingly easier. The entire substrate is already bits. You've got the internet as this giant corpus of humans doing knowledge work, you can run a million rollouts of a coding agent in parallel at basically zero marginal cost, and when the model makes a mistake nothing breaks in the real world. So you get these very fast loops. That's why we're seeing coding and a lot of the text-based stuff move so quickly. I think of a lot of knowledge work as "digital tasks that have a clear verifier," and anywhere you have that, progress is going to be really fast.

The physical world is just a fundamentally harder regime, and I think people underestimate this. There's no internet of robot experience sitting there. You have to go collect the data, and collecting it is slow and expensive because it runs at the speed of physics. You can't fast-forward reality. Every episode costs real time, real hardware, and sometimes a broken gripper. Simulation helps, and I'm actually fairly optimistic about sim-to-real improving, but the gap is stubborn because the world is messy in ways that are hard to model: friction, deformable objects, lighting, all of it.

The other thing I'd say is that Moravec's paradox is still very much alive. The stuff that feels hard to us, like writing code or doing math, turns out to be the easy part for these systems. The stuff a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a cup they've never seen, is the frontier. That's because evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on sensorimotor control and only a very short time on language and abstract reasoning. The neural net has to recapitulate all of that from a much smaller dataset.

So how does it actually play out? My guess is it's gradual and it's going to look less like humanoids everywhere overnight and more like a slow expansion of the perimeter. You start with structured environments where the variance is low, like warehouses and factories, where you can constrain the problem. Then you expand into semi-structured spaces. Homes are the hardest and probably last, just because every home is different and the tolerance for failure is very low. Nobody wants a robot that's right 95% of the time around their kids.

I also think the digital progress is upstream of the physical progress in a useful way. The vision-language models we're building are turning out to be a really good prior for robotics. They give the robot a world model, common sense about what objects are and what people want, and that was the piece that was missing for decades. So the capabilities transfer. It's the same recipe, large neural nets trained on lots of data, just with a much slower data flywheel.

If I had to put a rough shape on it, I'd say the digital transformation is a this-decade phenomenon and it's happening much faster than most people expected, and the physical one is a multi-decade thing that will feel slow and then suddenly not slow. I'd be careful about the demos, though. A demo is one data point. The real question is always the tail, and in the physical world the tail is where all the difficulty lives.

r002.rationale: It compares the pace and difficulty of digital and physical AI, but makes no claim that the physical-world AI market could be larger.

astra-6.text:
I think the digital world comes first because everything is already in the format these systems can work with. If you’re writing code, you can make a change, run it, get feedback, and try again. You can do that very quickly, and you can have many attempts happening in parallel.

The physical world makes that loop much harder. You need hardware, you need to collect data, things break, and a mistake can actually have consequences. You can’t necessarily speed up an experiment by a factor of a thousand. So even if the intelligence improves very quickly, deployment has this other clock associated with it.

But I’m excited about robotics because so much of what makes a robot useful is understanding the world: What am I looking at? What is someone asking me to do? What should happen next? We’re getting much better at those pieces. You still have to connect them to reliable perception and control, which is a substantial challenge.

I’d expect that to show up first in fairly constrained environments, where you can make the task and the surroundings predictable. A robot that can walk into anyone’s home and do anything is a much higher bar. There’s a lot of opportunity between where we are today and that endpoint.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the digital world comes first because it’s so much easier to work in. Everything is already represented inside a computer, actions are relatively cheap, and you can run lots of experiments in parallel. If an agent makes a mistake in a browser, you can often reset and try again. In the physical world, a mistake can break something, and collecting another example might require an actual robot to spend actual time doing it.

So I would expect a lot of the near-term opportunity to be in digital work: writing software, working with documents, operating tools. But that also helps build the foundations for physical work. You need perception, planning, memory, and the ability to recover when something unexpected happens. Those capabilities are useful in both settings.

The interesting question for robotics is how much of that intelligence transfers, and how much still has to be learned through interaction with the world. You can learn a lot from video, but watching someone manipulate an object doesn’t tell you exactly what forces to apply or what to do when it slips.

My expectation is that we’ll see progress first in environments where the task and the surroundings are fairly constrained. A general-purpose robot in someone’s home is a much harder proposition. I’m excited about it, but I think there’s a lot of valuable digital work to automate while we figure out that physical interface.
